candidateRows: Agnosticism is appropriate because God's nonexistence cannot be established, although a traditional creator remains improbable.
This establishes the skeptical position against which the debate's proposed evidence for Christian theism must be measured.
Asked to state his current position, O'Connor distinguishes uncertainty from ordinary atheist identification and explains his skeptical leaning.
Christian commitment can be rational despite uncertainty when accumulated considerations make it sufficiently credible to ground one's life.
The account defines Collins's epistemic posture: Christianity is not certain or demonstrable, but is credible enough for committed belief.
Collins describes belief as a spectrum, recounts his transition from atheism during medical training, and identifies Jesus as his enduring anchor.
God provides evidence sufficient for a free personal decision rather than coercive mathematical proof that would compel belief.
This supplies the governing evidential standard for Collins's case and explains why the absence of demonstrative proof does not defeat theism.
Collins distinguishes evidence from proof and argues that noncoercive evidence better fits a relationship involving love, trust, and voluntary decision.
The universe's beginning, fine-tuned constants, and mathematically beautiful laws collectively point toward an intelligence behind nature.
These cosmological and fine-tuning considerations constitute a principal affirmative route from the observed universe to an intelligent creator.
Collins cites cosmic origins, life-permitting constants, the comparative cost of a multiverse, and elegant physical equations as evidence of intelligence.
Objective morality, radical altruism, and experiences of beauty support theism beyond the more limited inference to a deistic intelligence.
The move attempts to bridge the gap from a generic creator to the personal and value-grounding God required by the affirmative position.
Collins argues that evolutionary psychology inadequately explains admired altruism and that profound beauty resists reduction, jointly motivating his leap of trust.
Claims about evidence for God are difficult to evaluate because the referent of God is incomprehensible without relying on contested revelation.
This challenges the intelligibility and testability of the debate's central hypothesis before any proposed evidence can establish Christian theism.
Collins's preceding claim that several observable considerations provide evidence for a divine intelligence and theism.
O'Connor argues that classical descriptions place God beyond ordinary predicates and that meaningful analogies depend on scriptural authority he does not accept.
Christianity undermines its own moral argument when scripture conflicts with the same moral intuitions invoked to lead people toward God.
The argument directly contests the transition from generic theism to Christianity by turning Collins's moral evidence against Christian scripture.
Collins's claim that moral awareness and admired radical altruism are evidence supporting theism and his Christian commitment.
O'Connor contrasts the moral intuition used to support God with troubling biblical material and argues that the resulting contradiction blocks Christianity.
Life-permitting physical constants require explanation, and an intelligent creator is less faith-demanding than an unobservable multiverse.
This is the developed affirmative fine-tuning argument, connecting physical sensitivity, cosmic complexity, and explanatory comparison to a creator.
Collins explains how small changes in gravity and other constants prevent complexity, then argues that their precision calls for intelligence and an uncaused cause.
Fine-tuning may count against classical theism because an unconstrained creator should not need a thought-permitting universe balanced on a narrow physical knife edge.
The move attacks the fine-tuning inference at its foundation by arguing that physical fragility is unexpected under an omnipotent creator hypothesis.
Collins's argument that narrowly life-permitting constants cry out for explanation by an intelligent creator rather than a multiverse.
O'Connor asks whether God is constrained by the constants and why a creator could not realize an equally interesting universe under different physical arrangements.
Fine-tuning is compatible with rival creator stories and may backfire against a benevolent omnipotent creator who wants a material universe.
By supplying a contrasting Gnostic creator explanation, the move challenges both the specificity and expectedness of fine-tuning under Christian theism.
Collins's inference that the precise life-permitting structure of this universe favors a purposeful and intelligent creator.
O'Connor uses a Gnostic demiurge scenario and a selection analogy to argue that extreme material improbability does not uniquely support the Christian creator.

Fine-tuning need not identify a uniquely possible universe, because multiple viable configurations may exist and God may select an especially complex, interesting one as an artist selects a masterpiece.
This directly defends the fine-tuning case against the objection that a creator's need to tune extremely narrow conditions counts against divine power or intention.
O'Connor's claim that extreme fine-tuning can count against a creator who freely wants a material universe.

O'Connor argues that overwhelmingly hostile possible conditions make fine-tuning potentially disconfirming; Collins replies that viable solutions need not be unique and portrays creation as artistic selection.
If God cannot produce the same life-permitting outcome with a stronger gravitational constant, then physical parameters constrain divine creative power in a way unlike ordinary theistic omnipotence.
The move attacks the coherence and evidential force of fine-tuning by arguing that Collins's explanation appears to subordinate an omnipotent creator to contingent physical parameters.
Collins's claim that God selected precise constants to create an interesting, complex, life-permitting universe.

After Collins describes complexity and conscious relationship as interesting divine goals, O'Connor asks whether God could realize those goals under different gravity or is constrained by the constants.
God's commitment to an orderly universe and loving relationships with complex creatures makes precise physical parameters the means to a chosen end, rather than an objectionable external constraint.
This supplies Collins's principal reconciliation of fine-tuning with divine power by grounding stable laws and life-permitting constants in God's nature and relational purpose.
O'Connor's argument that dependence on a particular gravitational value imposes a troubling physical limit on God's creative power.
O'Connor presses whether God could avoid a big crunch while changing gravity; Collins answers that divine order, love, and relational purposes guide the selection of lawful physical means.

Physical constants do not resemble logical necessities, so God's inability to create a life-permitting universe with different gravity would challenge omnipotence rather than merely exclude a contradiction.
The distinction between logical and physical impossibility sharpens the principal skeptical objection to using fine-tuned constants as evidence for an omnipotent designer.
Collins's suggestion that even God could not obtain complexity after changing one constant while retaining the remaining physical laws.
Collins compares the proposed alternative with making two plus two equal five; O'Connor replies that changed gravity is physically problematic but not logically self-contradictory.

Although fine-tuning gives some support to theism, the vast, lifeless universe and the immense evolutionary suffering of animals are substantially more expected under mindless natural development than under a loving creator.
This is a comparative worldview argument that grants the pro side's strongest cosmological evidence while presenting animal suffering as powerful counterevidence favoring skeptical agnosticism.
Collins's fine-tuning argument and his claim that God seeks loving relationships with complex creatures through an ordered creation.

The discussion moves from fine-tuning toward evil; O'Connor weighs observations under both hypotheses and argues that natural selection's scale and brutality resist standard free-will and soul-making defenses.
Evolution is an elegant lawful process consistent with a God of order, and its suffering does not show blind randomness because the life-producing outcome was built into the plan from the beginning.
This is Collins's primary defense against the evidential problem of evolutionary suffering and connects biological history to his broader case for orderly, purposeful creation.
O'Connor's claim that brutal evolutionary animal suffering is expected on atheism but inexplicable under a loving creator.

O'Connor ends with a vivid comparison involving becoming a random wild animal; Collins grants a hard problem but stresses beauty, limited animal mortality awareness, lawful evolution, and planned outcomes.

Appealing to an unknown divine explanation for suffering licenses an analogous unknown natural explanation for fine-tuning, while readily conceivable less-predatory ecosystems undermine claims that extreme animal suffering was necessary.
The move simultaneously weakens the fine-tuning inference and rebuts the ordered-evolution defense, connecting two of the debate's principal evidential considerations in favor of skepticism.
Collins's reliance on an unexplained divine plan and his contention that orderly evolution accounts for the observed history of animal life.

Collins says evolutionary outcomes were planned despite apparent randomness; O'Connor answers that mystery cannot be used asymmetrically and argues that herbivory or other systemic changes could reduce suffering.

So-called physical evil follows from stable natural laws, and avoiding it would require continual supernatural intervention; God judged the advent of relational human creatures worth that unavoidable cost.
This is a direct theistic justification of natural suffering based on law-governed creation, nonintervention, and the claimed value of conscious beings capable of relationship with God.
O'Connor's argument that an omnipotent deity could design an ecosystem without billions of years of agonizing predation and disease.

O'Connor argues that familiar predatory suffering was unnecessary and perhaps not worth humanity's emergence; Collins answers that physical harms accompany stable laws unless God constantly intervenes.

The central problem is not death or all suffering but the system's extreme depth of suffering, which a creator could reduce through general biological design without selectively intervening in individual cases.
The move directly counters the nonintervention defense by distinguishing ad hoc miracles from initial system design and by identifying plausible broad mechanisms for reducing animal agony.
Collins's claim that physical suffering is an unavoidable consequence of stable laws unless God intervenes continually in particular events.
Collins says lawful creation makes physical evil unavoidable and worth the emergence of humans; O'Connor focuses on acute animal fear and proposes herbivory or natural anesthetic mechanisms.

The historical existence and crucifixion of Jesus, reports of the empty tomb and risen appearances, and witnesses who maintained their testimony make resurrection the most likely explanation despite its miraculous character.
The resurrection is an expressly named pillar of the motion, and this passage supplies Collins's central positive historical case along with his explanation of divine suspension of natural laws.
Following discussion of suffering and the transition to Christianity's account of the cross, Collins presents historical, testimonial, and theological considerations supporting a real resurrection.
The Gospel accounts contain substantial legendary and theological development, giving reason to doubt their historical reliability.
This establishes O'Connor's foundational objection to treating the Gospel narratives as dependable evidence for Christianity and the resurrection.
Collins's preceding contention that the resurrection is the most likely explanation of the historical evidence.
After Collins presents the resurrection as compelling and compatible with divine suspension of natural laws, O'Connor challenges the underlying sources.
Independent corroboration across distinct Gospel sources raises historical confidence, while single-source stories warrant substantially less confidence.
The proposed corroboration test supplies the evidential method supporting O'Connor's later doubts about specific resurrection narratives.
The request to explain what evidence and sources justify O'Connor's judgments about the Gospel narratives.
O'Connor distinguishes the Synoptic dependencies, hypothetical source traditions, and John before comparing widely attested events with isolated stories.
O'Connor's skeptical prior leads him to discount unique Gospel testimony where a more receptive prior can regard it as credible.
Collins contests the neutrality of O'Connor's historical method by arguing that prior commitments shape how isolated testimony is evaluated.
O'Connor's claim that stories found in only one Gospel source deserve materially lower historical confidence.
Following the discussion of Doubting Thomas and source corroboration, Collins shifts attention from textual frequency to the interpreters' contrasting priors.
Genre, authorial theological purpose, multiple attestation, and potentially embarrassing material provide grounds for ranking Gospel claims by historical confidence.
This supplies a fuller methodology for separating probable historical material from later theology, including doubts about Jesus explicitly claiming divinity.
Collins's criticism that skeptical priors unfairly turn unique Gospel material into grounds for disbelief.
O'Connor denies that unique material is automatically false, then uses genre, authorial aims, attestation, and awkward traditions to compare claims.
The increasingly elaborate post-resurrection appearances in later Gospels are better explained as mythological development than as progressively detailed history.
This directly challenges the resurrection evidence at the center of Collins's Christian case by offering a natural historical explanation of the accounts.
Collins's request for O'Connor's interpretation of the events following the historically accepted crucifixion of Jesus.
O'Connor compares the earliest ending of Mark with later Gospel appearances and argues that detail, witnesses, and theology grow over time.
Traditions about the disciples' martyrdom are historically uncertain, and Paul's early testimony is weaker than bodily eyewitness testimony because his experience was visionary.
The move answers two principal resurrection defenses: sincere martyrdom and Paul's early testimony, disputing both their establishment and evidential force.
Collins's reliance on apostolic martyrdom and early resurrection testimony as support for the reality of Jesus's resurrection.
O'Connor questions the historical basis for claims about the disciples' deaths, then distinguishes Paul's visionary encounter from a bodily encounter with Jesus.
Atheistic certainty exceeds human epistemic limits, while cosmic order, objective moral orientation, Jesus's teaching, and the resurrection cumulatively support Christian faith.
This is Collins's cumulative positive case connecting limited human knowledge, fine-tuning, morality, Scripture, Jesus, and resurrection to Christian theism.
O'Connor's invitation for Collins to identify the priors and commitments he brings when interpreting the Gospel accounts.
Collins explains his departure from atheism, argues for a transcendent source of order and goodness, and defends a holistic reception of Christianity.
Personal and moral routes to Christianity can be legitimate for the believer, but public historical claims about resurrection still require exacting evidential scrutiny.
This distinguishes private justification from public evidence, preserving O'Connor's resurrection critique while acknowledging non-argumentative pathways to faith.
Collins's claim that Christianity's cumulative personal truth can reasonably be embraced without certainty on every historical detail.
O'Connor accepts that people often approach the Gospels after moral, social, or personal experiences, but explains why a skeptic must test resurrection evidence.
A specific, unwelcome message received during prayer can reasonably be treated as revelation when it seems unlike self-generated thought and transforms one's priorities.
The personal account advances revelation as an additional epistemic route to Christian belief beyond purely logical or scientific argument.
After discussion of whether belief must be purely rational, Collins describes a pointed prayer experience and its lasting practical and spiritual consequences.
Personal revelation could legitimately ground belief for its recipient, whereas philosophical argument alone is unlikely to convert and risks making divine access unfairly elitist.
The move defines O'Connor's conditions for changing his mind while explaining why private experience may have greater religious force than public argument.
Collins's account of receiving a specific message in prayer and his question about what revelation could change O'Connor's mind.
O'Connor says an isolated ambiguous message would shift confidence little, but a striking theological revelation could warrant belief for the experiencer.
The painful, unsettled character of aesthetic experience may reflect awareness that reality falls short of how it ought to be, rather than straightforward evidence for God.
This supplies the skeptical side's substantive interpretation of beauty, reframing a major theistic consideration without denying the experience itself.
Collins's suggestion that numinous encounters with music and art can disclose a transcendent divine reality.
After distinguishing several meanings of beauty, O'Connor examines its emotional phenomenology and connects aesthetic longing with suffering, absence, and perceived teleology.
Beauty can feel suggestive of a reality beyond ordinary experience and thus qualify as experiential evidence, but treating it as a direct argument for God is too crude.
The move gives the skeptical side's mature concession on beauty: it preserves evidential suggestiveness while resisting a decisive inference to theism.
The earlier Christian claim that beauty, music, and numinous longing point toward God seeking relationship with human beings.
O'Connor recounts being cautioned against overanalyzing beauty, acknowledges the force of aesthetic experience, and weighs its possible evidential significance while retaining skepticism.
Evolutionary functions for musical perception do not remove its divine significance, because human brains may be intended to make otherwise inaccessible revelation possible.
This directly answers a naturalistic explanation of beauty and preserves the pro side's claim that evolved mechanisms can mediate divine disclosure.
O'Connor's suggestion that aesthetic capacities may admit an evolutionary account and therefore need not require a divine explanation.
Collins describes specialized neural processing for music and its social functions, then argues that mechanistic or evolutionary explanation is compatible with theological purpose.
Fine-tuning, suffering, beauty, and the resurrection remain profound mysteries, so strong confidence about what they establish concerning God deserves suspicion.
This is the skeptical side's overarching conclusion across nearly every consideration named in the motion and states its governing epistemic standard.
The cumulative Christian case that fine-tuning, resurrection, revelation, and beauty jointly make confident theistic belief reasonable.
Following agreement that reductionist accounts do not dissolve aesthetic mystery, O'Connor generalizes that uncertainty across the debate's major arguments and counsels epistemic humility.
God's existence is the most important question because either ignoring a caring God or devoting oneself to a nonexistent God would profoundly misdirect one's life.
The move explains the practical stakes of the entire motion and grounds the pro side's demand that the question receive serious personal investigation.
Collins invokes the consequences on both sides of the existence question, recalls a patient's challenge to his former indifference, and describes both participants as continuing seekers.
The God question is intellectually compelling because it opens inquiry across science, ethics, history, art, and scripture, while Christianity cannot coherently be only moderately important.
This establishes why skeptical agnosticism still treats the motion seriously and distinguishes uncertainty about truth from indifference to the inquiry.
O'Connor agrees that both speakers remain on an uncertain road, then argues that discussion of God spans many disciplines and that Christianity is either momentous or false.
Even an atheist has reason to investigate Christianity because the possibility that it is true carries consequences large enough to justify continued inquiry.
The final substantive move articulates common ground between the sides and explains why skeptical nonbelief remains compatible with sustained engagement with the motion.
O'Connor contrasts the importance of the God question under theism and atheism, then gives a prudential reason for atheists to keep examining the possibility of Christianity.
